Ledgerly uses Django as its backend framework with Django REST Framework (DRF) for the REST API. The application is structured as a single Django monolith with a React frontend that communicates with the DRF API.
The team decided to store all money as integer cents in bigint columns, never as floats or Decimal in the database. Rounding happens once, when they render the invoice.

Based on session s14-mollie from June 17, 2026, Ledgerly switched all payments from Stripe to Mollie because Mollie's flat-fee model is much cheaper for invoices above 100 euros. New customers have been going to Mollie since that date.

Based on the session transcript, the team moved away from Stripe because Stripe charges a percentage on SEPA Direct Debit transactions, while Mollie charges a flat fee per transaction—which is much cheaper for invoices above 100 euros. This change was made because most of their invoices are above that threshold, making the flat fee structure more cost-effective.
Invoice numbers follow the format LDG-YYYY-NNNNN (e.g., LDG-2026-00042), with the counter resetting annually and no gaps allowed per German tax rules.

Invoice numbers must have no gaps because of German tax rules (GoBD), which do not allow holes in the numbering sequence. To ensure compliance, the team allocates invoice numbers inside the same transaction that finalizes the invoice.

The team switched to WeasyPrint because Puppeteer (headless Chrome) was crashing due to requiring more than the 512 MB memory available in their container. WeasyPrint renders HTML templates directly without needing a browser, making it much more lightweight for their resource-constrained environment.
The tests run against a real PostgreSQL database started with testcontainers. The team made this decision because using SQLite in tests previously hid bugs with bigint and row locking.

The server was taking invoice dates from UTC timestamps, which resulted in dates one day too early when customers finalized invoices shortly after midnight in their local timezone. The fix was to derive the `issued_on` date from the Europe/Berlin local date and add a test for 00:30 local time.

The team chose Postmark over SendGrid because in testing, SendGrid emails landed in spam at GMX and web.de—the email providers most of their German customers use. Postmark didn't have this deliverability issue.
Based on the session transcript from s08-auth, users log in to Ledgerly with magic links sent by email; the system does not store passwords, and links expire after 15 minutes and work once.

No, the team no longer uses Unleash. In session s13, they determined Unleash was overkill and required monthly server updates, so they replaced all feature flags with environment variables read at startup.

They added an idempotency key on the payment intent ID with a unique constraint, so a retried webhook becomes a no-op. This prevents duplicate payments from being created when Stripe retries a webhook after a timeout.
The Pro plan costs 29 euros per month. According to the team's pricing session (s11-pricing), the Pro plan also adds automatic dunning and custom invoice templates compared to the Starter tier.
Dunning reminders are sent 7, 14, and 30 days after the due date, with the first two being friendly reminders and the third reminder adding a 5-euro late fee.
The public API allows **60 requests per minute per API key**, with a 429 status code and Retry-After header returned when exceeded.

Database backups are kept for 30 days—nightly pg_dump backups are stored in S3-compatible object storage at Hetzner and retained for that period, with monthly restore tests performed on the first Monday of each month.
The team uses **i18next** for translations. This was mentioned in session s17-i18n where the user noted that they wrap every UI string with i18next instead of hardcoding German text.
Ledgerly uses Django with Django REST Framework as its backend, deployed as a single monolith. The team made this decision to keep the architecture simple while they're just two developers.

We store all money as integer cents in bigint columns, never as floats or Decimal types in the database. This approach avoids floating-point precision issues that can cause rounding errors in financial calculations.
Ledgerly uses Stripe as the payment provider for card payments for new customers. This decision has been consistently maintained across recent development sessions.

Stripe charged a percentage on SEPA Direct Debit transactions, while Mollie charges a flat fee per transaction, which is much cheaper for invoices above 100 euros. The team migrated new customers to Mollie starting in June 2026, with existing Stripe mandates migrated by the end of July.
Invoice numbers follow the format **LDG-YYYY-NNNNN** (e.g., LDG-2026-00042), with the counter resetting every January. Numbers must be gapless to comply with German tax rules (GoBD).
German tax rules (GoBD) do not allow gaps in invoice numbers. The team allocates invoice numbers inside the same transaction that finalizes the invoice to ensure they remain gapless.

Puppeteer (headless Chrome) was crashing due to memory constraints in your 512 MB container environment. WeasyPrint was chosen as a lighter alternative that renders HTML templates directly without requiring a browser.
Tests run against a real PostgreSQL database started with testcontainers. The team switched from SQLite to Postgres because SQLite was hiding bugs with bigint and row locking.

The server was running in UTC and the team was deriving the invoice date from a UTC timestamp, which caused dates to be one day early when customers finalized invoices shortly after midnight in their local timezone. The fix was to derive `issued_on` from the Europe/Berlin local date instead and add a test for 00:30 local time.

The team chose Postmark over SendGrid because in testing, SendGrid emails landed in spam at GMX and web.de, which most of their German customers use. Postmark had better deliverability for their target audience.
Users log in to Ledgerly with magic links sent to their email; the platform does not store passwords at all, and links expire after 15 minutes and work once.
No, the team removed Unleash in June 2026 because it was overkill and required monthly server updates. They replaced it with environment variables read at startup.

They added an idempotency key on the payment intent ID with a unique constraint so that when Stripe retried the webhook, the second attempt would be a no-op. This prevented duplicate payment records from being created on webhook retries after timeouts.
The Pro plan costs 29 euros per month and includes automatic dunning and custom invoice templates.
Dunning reminders are sent 7, 14, and 30 days after the due date. The first two are friendly reminders without a fee, while the third reminder adds a late fee of 5 euros.
The public API rate limit is 60 requests per minute per API key. Requests exceeding this limit receive a 429 status code with a Retry-After header.
The team keeps database backups for 30 days, stored nightly via pg_dump to S3-compatible object storage at Hetzner, with restore tests conducted on the first Monday of every month.
Ledgerly uses **i18next** for translations. The team wraps every string with i18next instead of hardcoding text.
